newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Congressional panel proposes IRS shake-up.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Congressional panel proposes IRS shake-up.

text.p: A bipartisan Congressional commission Thursday endorsed a sweeping plan to shake up the troubled Internal Revenue Service and simplify the 9,451-page tax code that it administers.
"We need to truly create a new IRS," Republican Rep. Rob Portman from Ohio told reporters. "It is not working well," Portman, co-chairman of the commission, added.

The plan, which will be formally released later this month, includes a controversial proposal to strip the Treasury Department of responsibility for overseeing IRS operations and replace it with an independent board -- a suggestion that Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin called "substantially flawed."

Among some of the other recommendations: a sharp increase in electronic filing of returns by taxpayers; restructuring of the IRS's relations with Congress, and establishment of a tax complexity index to measure prospective legislation.

Just over 15 percent of the 114 million individual income tax returns filed to the IRS this year came in electronically via telephone lines. The commission wants that to rise to 80 percent in 10 years, perhaps by extending the deadline for such returns past April 15.
Democratic Sen. Bob Kerrey from Nebraska, who also co-chaired the commission, said the panel wants to move quickly to translate the proposals into legislation.
But the commission is already running into flak from the Clinton administration over its proposal to create an independent board to oversee IRS operations.
"I do not think it's an effective way to go," Rubin told reporters at a separate briefing. "You can't take the risk of having the IRS not work, because it funds 95 percent of the federal government."

Under the commission's proposal, the seven-person board would be comprised of five private citizens appointed by the president and approved by the Senate, and two govermnment officials. The labor union representing IRS employees would also have a seat on the board.
The board would oversee the agency and appoint the IRS commissioner but would not get involved in tax cases.

Deputy Treasury Secretary Lawrence Summers declined to say whether President Clinton would veto legislation that included an independent board. "I don't think we're at that stage yet," he said. "We don't even have a bill."

The administration has put forward its own plan for improving operations of the IRS. Under that proposal, the president would name a board of government officials to oversee the tax collection agency. A separate board of private sector experts would also be established to provide advice.

The IRS has long been a favorite target of taxpayers and lawmakers who blame it for a tax code that many see as unfair and unwieldly. But it has come under particular attack recently for what is widely perceived as a bungled $4 billion effort to upgrade its technology and improve it service.

In its formal proposal later this month, the commission plans to present 60 specific ways to make the tax code simpler, including abolition of the alternative minimum tax, which aims to ensure that rich individuals with many deductions pay tax but has not raised much revenue.

The commission also proposed establishing a panel of lawmakers to deal directly with the IRS on budget and other matters. Right now, the agency is subject to jurisdiction of seven Congressional committees with no central point of contact.
